options.text: The movement of water across a membrane from an area of high water concentration to low
options.feedback: Correct -- osmosis moves water to balance concentration on both sides of a membrane.

options.text: The movement of sugar molecules only
options.feedback: Osmosis specifically refers to water movement, not sugar or other solutes.

options.text: The breakdown of food in the stomach
options.feedback: That describes digestion, an entirely different process.

options.text: The process of cell division
options.feedback: Cell division is mitosis or meiosis, unrelated to water movement across membranes.

medium.text: If a plant cell is placed in very salty water, what will likely happen to it?

options.text: Water will leave the cell, causing it to shrink
options.feedback: Correct -- water moves out toward the higher salt concentration outside, causing the cell to lose water.

options.text: Water will rush into the cell, causing it to swell and burst
options.feedback: This would happen in very fresh (low-salt) water, not salty water.

options.text: Nothing will happen to the cell at all
options.feedback: A significant concentration difference like this will cause water movement, not no change.

options.text: The cell will start photosynthesizing faster
options.feedback: Salt concentration affects water balance, not photosynthesis rate directly.

hard.text: Two solutions are separated by a membrane permeable only to water. Solution A has a higher solute concentration than Solution B. In which direction will water move?

options.text: From Solution B into Solution A
options.feedback: Correct -- water moves toward the solution with more dissolved solute (lower water concentration) to balance things out.

options.text: From Solution A into Solution B
options.feedback: This is the reverse of the actual direction -- water moves toward the higher-solute side, not away from it.

options.text: Water won't move in either direction
options.feedback: A concentration difference across a water-permeable membrane will cause net water movement.

options.text: Water moves equally in both directions with no net change
options.feedback: While water molecules move both ways, there is a net flow toward the higher-solute solution until balance is reached.

easy.hard: This process specifically involves water molecules crossing a selectively permeable barrier.
easy.medium: This is when water moves through a membrane to even out concentration on both sides.
easy.easy: This is when water moves through a membrane from where there's more water to where there's less.

medium.hard: Water will move toward the side with the higher concentration of dissolved particles, leaving the cell in this scenario.
medium.medium: Water moves toward the saltier side, which means it will leave the cell.
medium.easy: Water tends to move out of the cell and into the saltier water outside.

hard.hard: Water flows toward the solution with the greater solute concentration (and thus lower water concentration) in an effort to equalize concentrations on both sides.
hard.medium: Water always moves toward the side with more dissolved solute, since that side effectively has less water.
hard.easy: Water moves toward the side that has more dissolved stuff in it -- that's Solution A.

easy.text: If a dominant allele and a recessive allele are both present, which trait is usually expressed?

options.text: The dominant trait
options.feedback: Correct -- a dominant allele masks the effect of a recessive one when both are present.

options.text: The recessive trait
options.feedback: The recessive trait is masked when a dominant allele is present.

options.text: Both traits blend together equally
options.feedback: Simple dominant/recessive inheritance doesn't blend traits -- the dominant one is expressed.

options.text: Neither trait is expressed
options.feedback: One of the two alleles is always expressed in this simple inheritance pattern -- specifically the dominant one.

medium.text: For a recessive trait to be physically expressed in an organism, what must be true of its alleles?

options.text: Both alleles must be the recessive version
options.feedback: Correct -- a recessive trait only shows up when there's no dominant allele present to mask it.

options.text: Only one allele needs to be recessive
options.feedback: A single recessive allele paired with a dominant one would be masked -- both must be recessive.

options.text: Both alleles must be dominant
options.feedback: Two dominant alleles would express the dominant trait, not the recessive one.

options.text: The organism must have no alleles for that trait
options.feedback: Organisms always have two alleles for a given trait (one from each parent) -- the trait isn't simply absent.

hard.text: Two parents who are both heterozygous (carrying one dominant and one recessive allele) for a trait have a child. What is the probability the child shows the recessive trait?

options.feedback: Correct -- a Punnett square cross of two heterozygous parents gives a 1-in-4 chance of the recessive-recessive combination.
50% would be the chance of being heterozygous like the parents, not the chance of showing the recessive trait.
75% is actually the chance the child shows the DOMINANT trait, not the recessive one.
Since both parents carry a dominant allele too, the recessive trait isn't guaranteed to appear.

easy.hard: This type of allele's effect shows up even when only one copy is present alongside a different version.
easy.medium: This is the version of a gene that gets expressed whenever it's present, even alongside a different version.
easy.easy: This is the stronger version of a gene that shows up whenever it's present.

medium.hard: This weaker version of a gene is hidden by a dominant allele, only showing itself when no dominant version is around.
medium.medium: This weaker gene version only shows up when there's no dominant allele hiding it.
medium.easy: The weaker gene version only shows up when both copies are the weaker version.

hard.hard: Cross the two heterozygous genotypes in a Punnett square -- one out of the four resulting combinations pairs two recessive alleles together.
hard.medium: Draw out a Punnett square for two heterozygous parents -- count how many of the four boxes show two recessive alleles.
hard.easy: In a Punnett square for two heterozygous parents, only 1 of the 4 boxes has two recessive alleles.

options.text: The natural process by which nitrogen moves between the atmosphere, soil, and living things
options.feedback: Correct -- the nitrogen cycle describes nitrogen's movement through ecosystems.

options.text: The process of plants absorbing sunlight
options.feedback: That describes part of photosynthesis, not the nitrogen cycle.

options.text: The way water evaporates and falls as rain
options.feedback: That describes the water cycle, a different natural cycle.

options.text: The breakdown of rocks over time
options.feedback: That describes weathering, unrelated to the nitrogen cycle.

medium.text: What role do nitrogen-fixing bacteria play in the nitrogen cycle?

options.text: They convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into a form plants can use
options.feedback: Correct -- most plants can't use nitrogen gas directly, so these bacteria convert it into usable compounds.

options.text: They convert oxygen into nitrogen gas
options.feedback: These bacteria work with nitrogen gas, not converting oxygen into it.

options.text: They release nitrogen gas from decomposing bodies
options.feedback: That's closer to the role of decomposers, not nitrogen-fixing bacteria specifically.

options.text: They allow plants to absorb sunlight more efficiently
options.feedback: Sunlight absorption relates to photosynthesis, not nitrogen fixation.

hard.text: Why can't most plants use the abundant nitrogen gas (N₂) that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere directly?

options.text: The triple bond holding N₂ together is very stable and hard for plants to break
options.feedback: Correct -- nitrogen gas's strong triple bond requires specialized bacteria (or lightning/industrial processes) to break it into usable forms.

options.text: Plants have no need for nitrogen at all
options.feedback: Plants actually need nitrogen for proteins and other essential molecules -- they just can't access the gas form directly.

options.text: Nitrogen gas is toxic to all plant roots
options.feedback: Nitrogen gas isn't toxic -- plants simply lack the biological mechanism to break its strong bond directly.

options.text: Nitrogen gas only exists deep underground, out of reach of roots
options.feedback: Nitrogen gas is actually abundant in the atmosphere above ground, not confined underground.

easy.hard: This describes the movement of one essential element between air, ground, and organisms.
easy.medium: This describes how one particular element moves between the air, the soil, and living organisms.
easy.easy: This is the natural cycle describing how nitrogen moves through nature.

medium.hard: These organisms perform the crucial chemical conversion that unlocks atmospheric nitrogen for biological use.
medium.medium: These bacteria transform nitrogen from the air into a form that plant roots can actually absorb.
medium.easy: These bacteria change nitrogen from the air into a form plants can actually use.

hard.hard: The two nitrogen atoms in N₂ are joined by an unusually strong triple covalent bond, requiring significant energy or specialized enzymes to break apart.
hard.medium: The two nitrogen atoms in the gas are bonded together extremely tightly, and only certain bacteria have the tools to break that bond.
hard.easy: The nitrogen atoms in the gas are stuck together very tightly, and only special bacteria can break them apart.

easy.text: Which biome is characterized by extremely low precipitation and sparse vegetation?

options.text: Desert
options.feedback: Correct -- deserts receive very little rainfall and support only specially adapted plants.

options.text: Rainforest
options.feedback: Rainforests receive very high amounts of rainfall, the opposite of a desert.

options.text: Tundra
options.feedback: Tundra is defined more by extreme cold than by low precipitation specifically.

options.text: Wetland
options.feedback: Wetlands are saturated with water, the opposite of a dry desert environment.

medium.text: Which biome is known for its permanently frozen layer of subsoil called permafrost?

options.text: Tundra
options.feedback: Correct -- tundra biomes have a permafrost layer that stays frozen year-round.

options.text: Tropical rainforest
options.feedback: Rainforests are warm and humid, without any permanently frozen soil.

options.text: Grassland
options.feedback: Grasslands don't have a permanently frozen subsoil layer.

options.text: Desert
options.feedback: Deserts are defined by dryness, not by permanently frozen ground.

hard.text: A biome has high year-round rainfall, warm temperatures, and the greatest biodiversity of any land biome. Which biome is this most likely describing?

options.text: Tropical rainforest
options.feedback: Correct -- tropical rainforests combine consistent warmth and heavy rainfall to support the richest biodiversity on land.

options.text: Taiga (boreal forest)
options.feedback: Taiga has cold winters and lower biodiversity compared to tropical rainforests.

options.text: Desert
options.feedback: Deserts have very low rainfall, the opposite of this description.

options.text: Tundra
options.feedback: Tundra is cold with low biodiversity, not warm and rich in species.

easy.hard: This environment supports only plants adapted to conserve water due to minimal rainfall.
easy.medium: This dry environment gets very little rain all year long.
easy.easy: This is the very dry biome that gets hardly any rain.

medium.hard: This cold biome's ground stays frozen at depth even when the surface briefly thaws in summer.
medium.medium: This cold biome has ground that stays frozen deep down, even in summer.
medium.easy: This cold biome has ground that never fully thaws, even in summer.

hard.hard: Consistent warmth combined with abundant year-round rainfall creates ideal conditions for the highest species diversity among terrestrial biomes.
hard.medium: Warm temperatures plus heavy rain year-round create the richest variety of life among land biomes.
hard.easy: Warm and rainy all year round, with more types of plants and animals than anywhere else on land.

easy.text: What is the main function of the kidneys?

options.text: Filtering waste products out of the blood
options.feedback: Correct -- kidneys remove waste and excess substances from the blood to form urine.

options.text: Pumping blood throughout the body
options.feedback: That's the heart's job, not the kidneys'.

options.text: Breaking down food in the stomach
options.feedback: Food breakdown happens in the digestive system, not the kidneys.

options.text: Producing sound for speech
options.feedback: Sound production involves the vocal cords, unrelated to kidney function.

medium.text: What waste product do the kidneys filter out that comes from protein breakdown?

options.text: Urea
options.feedback: Correct -- urea is a nitrogen-containing waste product from protein breakdown, filtered by the kidneys into urine.

options.text: Glucose
options.feedback: Glucose is generally reabsorbed by the kidneys, not treated as a waste product to remove.

options.text: Oxygen
options.feedback: Oxygen is a needed gas the body uses, not a waste product filtered by the kidneys.

options.text: Calcium
options.feedback: Calcium is an important mineral the body regulates, not primarily a waste product from protein breakdown.

hard.text: Which structure within the kidney is primarily responsible for filtering blood to begin forming urine?

options.text: Nephron
options.feedback: Correct -- nephrons are the kidney's microscopic filtering units where blood filtration and urine formation begin.

options.text: Bladder
options.feedback: The bladder stores urine after it's already been formed -- it doesn't do the filtering itself.

options.text: Ureter
options.feedback: The ureter is a tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder, not a filtering structure.

options.text: Esophagus
options.feedback: The esophagus is part of the digestive system, entirely unrelated to kidney filtration.

easy.hard: This organ's job is to clean the blood, similar to how a filter cleans water.
easy.medium: This organ removes unwanted substances from the blood to make urine.
easy.easy: This organ cleans your blood and helps make urine.

medium.hard: This nitrogen-based waste molecule forms specifically when the body processes protein and needs to remove leftover nitrogen.
medium.medium: This waste product forms from breaking down proteins and needs to be removed from blood.
medium.easy: This is the waste product from digesting protein that ends up in urine.

hard.hard: This is the kidney's basic functional and filtering unit, present by the thousands in each kidney, where blood pressure forces fluid out for initial filtration.
hard.medium: This tiny structure inside the kidney is where the actual blood filtering happens, not the storage or tube structures nearby.
hard.easy: This tiny structure inside the kidney does the actual filtering job, not the tubes or storage parts.
